title: A nuclear reactor’s blue glow comes from particles outrunning light in water

cover.alt: The core of the Advanced Test Reactor at Idaho National Laboratory, seen through the water of its pool, glowing an intense blue.

body: Nothing beats light in a vacuum, but in water light slows to **about 0.75 of its vacuum speed**. Charged particles from a reactor, such as fast electrons, can move faster than that while still staying below the cosmic limit. A charged particle that outruns light in a material sheds a cone of light, much as a supersonic jet leaves a sonic boom. This Cherenkov radiation grows stronger at higher frequencies, so most of it is ultraviolet and the part we can see looks brilliant blue.

slides.question: In water, light travels at what share of its speed in a vacuum?
slides.explanation: About 75%, because water’s refractive index is about 1.33. A charged particle moving faster than that, though still slower than light in a vacuum, gives off Cherenkov light.

left.label: Sounds like
left.text: The particles break Einstein’s speed limit.

right.label: Actually
right.text: They only beat light slowed down by water. Light in a vacuum, c, stays the limit, so relativity is safe.

steps.label: The reactor releases fast charged particles
They move faster than light does in water
They shed a cone of light, like a sonic boom
Mostly ultraviolet, so what we see is blue

slides.heading: A sonic boom made of light
slides.text: A jet faster than sound piles its sound waves into a cone-shaped shock front. A charged particle faster than light in a material does the same with light. The faster it goes, the wider the cone, so measuring the angle tells physicists how fast the particle was moving.

events.text: Marie Curie sees blue light in radium
Igor Tamm and Ilya Frank explain it
All three share the Nobel Prize

slides.heading: Why physicists love it
slides.text: Cherenkov light is used to identify particles in accelerator experiments, to catch neutrinos in giant water tanks such as Super-Kamiokande, to check that spent fuel really sits in a reactor’s storage pool, and even to image radiotherapy beams inside patients.

slides.question: Why does Cherenkov light look blue rather than red?
options: It grows stronger at higher frequencies
slides.explanation: Its strength rises with frequency, so most of it is ultraviolet. Of the part our eyes can see, the blue end is the brightest.
